label: Duke of Kent begins the Great Garden
more: In 1706, the year he became Marquess of Kent, Henry Grey began adding a French-style formal woodland round his parents' Long Water: straight avenues, clearings, statues and canals on three sides. English Heritage says the work ran into the 1720s.

label: Henry Grey created Duke of Kent
more: The Marquess of Kent was made a duke in 1710, during the War of the Spanish Succession, in exchange for giving up his post as Lord Chamberlain. English Heritage thinks the Archer Pavilion's wall paintings celebrate the honour.

label: East and West Half Houses built
more: These two small garden shelters were built in clearings in the Duke's woodland, either side of the Long Water, when its avenues and squares were largely complete. Each has a curved wooden seat inside. The listings give no architect.

label: Bowling Green House by Batty Langley
more: Langley remodelled an earlier building into a pavilion with a six-column wooden portico facing the bowling green. The date is uncertain: about 1735 in the listing, 1735 (latest 1734) in Parks & Gardens UK, and English Heritage's plan dates the main walls 1720–1721.

label: Serpentine canal dug; amphitheatre added by the bowling green
more: When work resumed in 1729, the Duke's garden gained a serpentine canal and an amphitheatre north of the bowling green. Brown later joined the serpentine water to Old Park Water, about 1760.
